title: Oír vs Escuchar: Hear or Listen in Spanish?
seo_title: Oír vs Escuchar: Hear or Listen in Spanish?
meta_description: Oír vs escuchar: hearing vs listening in Spanish. The core rule, regional usage, the many meanings of ¡oye!, conjugation, mistakes and a quick quiz.
excerpt: Hearing happens to you; listening is something you do. Here’s how Spanish shows it.

body_html:
Oír vs escuchar works just like English “hear” and “listen”: oír is perceiving sound, whether you want to or not, and escuchar is paying attention to it. You oyes a dog barking; you escuchas a podcast. The pair is mostly straightforward, but regional habits, the very common interjection ¡oye! and an irregular conjugation make it worth a closer look.

Quick answer
  • Oír = to hear (perception, often involuntary).
  • Escuchar = to listen (attention, intention).
  • In much of Latin America, escuchar is also used for “hear”: No te escucho.
  • ¡Oye! means “Hey!” or “Listen!”
{{toc}}

Oír vs escuchar: the core rule

OírEscuchar
Meaningto hearto listen (to)
IntentionNot necessaryDeliberate
ExampleOí un ruido raro. I heard a strange noise.Escucho la radio por las mañanas. I listen to the radio in the mornings.

The RAE dictionary defines oír as perceiving sounds with the ear, and escuchar as applying your ear in order to hear. Like {{link:mirar-vs-ver|mirar vs ver}}, it is perception versus intention.

When to use oír

  • Sounds that reach you: ¿Oyes la lluvia? Can you hear the rain?
  • Ability to hear: Mi abuelo no oye bien. My grandfather doesn’t hear well.
  • Hearing news: He oído que te vas a mudar. I’ve heard you’re moving.
  • Getting attention: ¡Oye, espera! Hey, wait!

When to use escuchar

  • Music, radio, podcasts: ¿Qué música escuchas? What music do you listen to?
  • Paying attention: Escúchame, es importante. Listen to me, it’s important.
  • Taking advice: Nunca escucha a nadie. He never listens to anyone.
  • Emotional support: Gracias por escucharme. Thanks for listening to me.

Notice there is no preposition: escuchar música, not escuchar a música. Use a only before people: escuchar a tu madre.

{{image:2}}

Regional reality: escuchar for hearing

Textbooks keep the two verbs apart, but in everyday speech across much of Latin America, escuchar is often used where oír would be expected: No te escucho bien (I can’t hear you well) on the phone, or ¿Escuchaste eso? (Did you hear that?). In Spain, oír is more common in these cases: No te oigo. Both are understood everywhere; just be aware that the line is blurrier in real life than in grammar books.

All the meanings of ¡oye!

Oye (the tú command of oír) is one of the most frequent words in spoken Spanish:

  • Getting attention: ¡Oye, Marta! Hey, Marta!
  • Starting a topic: Oye, ¿qué haces el sábado? Hey, what are you doing on Saturday?
  • Mild protest: ¡Oye, que era mío! Hey, that was mine!
  • Formal version: Oiga, perdone… Excuse me… (usted)
{{book:love-slowly}}

Conjugation note

Oír is irregular and has a y in several forms: oigo, oyes, oye, oímos, oís, oyen; past oí, oíste, oyó, oímos, oyeron; gerund oyendo. Escuchar is regular.

Real conversations

On the phone

  • A: ¿Me oyes? Se corta un poco. (Can you hear me? It’s cutting out a bit.)
  • B: Ahora sí te oigo. Dime. (Now I can hear you. Go ahead.)

Between friends

  • A: Oye, ¿has escuchado el nuevo disco de Rosalía? (Hey, have you listened to Rosalía’s new album?)
  • B: He oído una canción en la radio, pero no lo he escuchado entero. (I heard one song on the radio, but I haven’t listened to the whole thing.)

That second line shows the pair perfectly: hearing a song by chance, versus listening to an album on purpose.

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Escucho a la música.Escucho música.No a before things
Oigo la radio cada mañana. (on purpose)Escucho la radio cada mañana.Deliberate listening
Oió / oíeronoyó / oyeronThe i becomes y
Escúchame que llegué.Oye, que ya llegué.Getting attention uses oye
{{image:3}}

Listening as a skill

For learners, escuchar is also a study method. Listening regularly to Spanish you can mostly understand is one of the best ways to improve; I explain why in {{link:comprehensible-input-spanish|comprehensible input}}. And in relationships, real listening is a gift: Me encanta que me escuches (I love that you listen to me). For more pairs, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

A cultural aside: in many Spanish-speaking households, the radio or TV is on in the background all day. That is oír in action. When the news comes on and everyone goes quiet, they switch to escuchar.

Try it yourself

Translate these sentences, then check your answers:

  1. I can’t hear you, the music is too loud. (No te oigo, la música está muy alta.)
  2. She listens to jazz when she works. (Escucha jazz cuando trabaja.)
  3. Have you heard the news? (¿Has oído la noticia?)
  4. Listen to me, please. (Escúchame, por favor.)
  5. Hey, do you have a minute? (Oye, ¿tienes un minuto?)

Notice how naturally oye opens the last sentence. Use it the next time you start a chat in Spanish.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Oír happens to you; escuchar is something you do. Keep that difference in mind, accept that many Latin Americans use escuchar for both, and remember that ¡oye! is your new favorite way to say “hey”.

faq.q: What is the difference between oír and escuchar?
faq.a: Oír means to hear, to perceive sound. Escuchar means to listen, to pay attention to sound deliberately.
In everyday Latin American Spanish, yes: No te escucho is common on the phone. In Spain, No te oigo is more usual.

faq.q: What does oye mean in Spanish?
faq.a: Oye is the tú command of oír and works like “hey” or “listen” to get attention or start a topic.
